concepts.why: A team gets consistent, safe results only when instructions, permissions and extensions are versioned and reviewed like code.
concepts.body:
On a team, every developer's Claude should follow the same conventions and safety rules. The tool supports this through layers you already know, used deliberately.

**Commit the shared layer.** The repository's `.claude/` folder holds `settings.json` (permissions, hooks, enabled plugins), `skills/`, `agents/` and `rules/`, next to `CLAUDE.md` and `.mcp.json`. Review changes to them in pull requests exactly like code: a new hook or MCP server runs on every teammate's machine. Personal tweaks stay in `.claude/settings.local.json`, `CLAUDE.local.md` and `~/.claude/`.

**Keep always-loaded context small.** In a large repo a single CLAUDE.md grows until rules get ignored. Split it:

- nested `CLAUDE.md` files in subprojects load only when Claude works there,
- `.claude/rules/*.md` with a `paths:` list in frontmatter load only for matching files,
- long procedures become skills,
- `claudeMdExcludes` skips other teams' instruction files in a **monorepo** (one big repository holding many projects).

If the repo also serves other agents, an `AGENTS.md` can be the shared file; a `CLAUDE.md` containing `@AGENTS.md` pulls it in and adds Claude-specific notes.

**Enforce with managed settings.** Organization admins can push out managed settings (as a file, through device-management software or from the claude.ai admin console) and a managed CLAUDE.md. Managed settings outrank everything else: required deny rules, sandbox enforcement, allowed models, disabling `bypassPermissions` or auto mode, and restricting which hooks, MCP servers and plugin marketplaces may run. Use managed settings for rules that must hold, and CLAUDE.md for guidance.

**Measure and adjust.** `/insights` reports how you use Claude Code and where sessions go wrong; usage dashboards and exported usage data cover whole teams. Prune instructions that no longer change behavior, and turn rules Claude keeps missing into hooks or permissions.
concepts.code:
repo/
├── CLAUDE.md                     # short: commands, conventions, gotchas
├── .mcp.json                     # shared MCP servers (reviewed in PRs)
├── .claude/
│   ├── settings.json             # team permissions, hooks, enabledPlugins
│   ├── rules/
│   │   ├── api.md                # frontmatter: paths: ["src/api/**/*.ts"]
│   │   └── testing.md
│   ├── skills/release/SKILL.md   # /release, disable-model-invocation: true
│   └── agents/reviewer.md        # fresh-context reviewer subagent
├── services/payments/CLAUDE.md   # loads only when working in payments/
└── .gitignore                    # CLAUDE.local.md, .claude/settings.local.json
takeaways: Commit .claude/ (settings, rules, skills, agents) and review it like code
Keep always-on context small with nested CLAUDE.md, path-scoped rules and skills
Managed settings enforce org policy; CLAUDE.md only guides
pitfalls: Merging a teammate's new project hook or MCP server without review, which then runs on everyone's machine.

quiz.q: A security rule must apply to every developer and must not be overridable. Where does it go?
options: Managed settings deployed by the organization
quiz.explain: Managed settings sit at the top of the precedence order and can't be overridden; CLAUDE.md is only guidance.

concepts.name: The Claude Agent SDK
concepts.summary: Embed Claude Code's agent loop, tools, permissions and hooks in your own Python or TypeScript program with the Agent SDK.
concepts.why: When a CLI script is not enough, the SDK lets you build custom agents on the same engine with full programmatic control.
concepts.body:
The **Claude Agent SDK** (formerly the Claude Code SDK) is Claude Code as a **library**: ready-made code your own program can load and call. It gives your program the same agent loop, built-in tools, context management, permissions, sessions, hooks, subagents, MCP support and skills, from Python or TypeScript. Compare the options:

- the **CLI** with `-p`: quickest for scripts and CI, callable from any language,
- the **Agent SDK**: an agent inside your own application; your code is called at each step and receives structured messages,
- the plain Claude API SDKs: you write the tool loop yourself.

In Python, install `claude-agent-sdk` (Python 3.10+); the TypeScript version is `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`. The main function, `query()`, is **asynchronous**: it hands you messages one at a time as the agent works, and your program can do other things while it waits. Messages include Claude's text, tool use, tool results and a final result with cost. Options go in `ClaudeAgentOptions`:

- `allowed_tools`: tools approved automatically (it does not remove others; use `disallowed_tools` for that),
- `permission_mode`: for example `acceptEdits` or `dontAsk`,
- `cwd`: the project directory,
- `system_prompt`, `max_turns`, MCP servers and more.

For two-way conversations, custom tools written as Python functions and hooks as functions in your own code, use `ClaudeSDKClient`. The SDK loads skills, commands and CLAUDE.md files from the project like the CLI does unless you configure otherwise.

Products you build sign in with an API key (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) or a cloud provider, not a personal claude.ai login. Treat an SDK agent like any program with shell access: run it in a container, give it only the tools and access it needs, cap turns and budget, and keep a record of its actions.
concepts.code:
# pip install claude-agent-sdk     (needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY)
import anyio
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, AssistantMessage, TextBlock

async def main():
    options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd="/srv/repos/billing",
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Bash(pytest *)"],
        permission_mode="dontAsk",      # anything not allowed is denied
        system_prompt="You are a careful maintenance bot. Never edit tests.",
        max_turns=15,
    )
    async for message in query(prompt="Run pytest and summarize failures by root cause",
                               options=options):
        if isinstance(message, AssistantMessage):
            for block in message.content:
                if isinstance(block, TextBlock):
                    print(block.text)

anyio.run(main)
takeaways: The Agent SDK exposes Claude Code's loop, tools, permissions and hooks as a library
Python: `query()` streams messages; configure it with `ClaudeAgentOptions`
`allowed_tools` auto-approves; it doesn't remove tools, so also set `permission_mode` or `disallowed_tools`
pitfalls: Assuming `allowed_tools` is a complete list that hides every other tool; unlisted tools fall through to the permission mode.

quiz.q: You need a custom agent inside a Python web service with callbacks for tool approval. Which fits best?
quiz.explain: The SDK embeds the agent loop in your process with programmatic control.

concepts.name: Parallel sessions and scaling up
concepts.summary: Run several Claude sessions in git worktrees, use writer/reviewer pairs, fan out claude -p over many files, and gate unattended runs with checks.
concepts.why: Once one session works well, running several at once and adding independent review multiplies output without multiplying mistakes.
concepts.body:
One well-run session is a good start; experts run several and make them check each other.

**Isolation**: two sessions editing the same checkout collide. Git **worktrees** give each session its own folder on its own branch from the same repository, so each runs its own `claude` safely. The desktop app and background sessions (`/background`, `claude agents`) offer the same idea in a visual app.

**Writer/reviewer**: a fresh context reviews better than the one that wrote the code, because it is not anchored on its own reasoning. Have session A implement, session B (or a subagent) review the diff against the plan, then feed findings back. Tell the reviewer to report only correctness and requirement gaps, or it will invent work. The bundled `/code-review` skill does a version of this.

**Fan-out** (splitting one big job into many small runs): for a change across hundreds of files, have Claude write the file list, then loop `claude -p` over it with tight `--allowedTools` and `--permission-mode dontAsk`. Run two or three files first, fix the prompt, then the rest. `/batch <instruction>` does this inside Claude Code, splitting work across subagents in separate worktrees.

**Gates for unattended work**: an unattended run needs a check that decides when it is done. Options from weakest to strongest: ask for the check in the prompt; set a `/goal` condition that an evaluator re-checks each turn; a `Stop` hook that runs tests and blocks finishing until they pass.

Costs grow with every extra context, so keep tasks small and self-contained. And keep humans on the merge: agents working side by side produce more diffs, which makes careful review more important, not less.
concepts.code:
# two isolated sessions on separate branches of one repo
git worktree add ../app-ratelimit -b feat/rate-limit
git worktree add ../app-review    -b review/rate-limit
(cd ../app-ratelimit && claude "implement the rate limiter from PLAN.md")
# later, in a fresh context:
(cd ../app-review && git merge feat/rate-limit && \
  claude "review this branch's diff against PLAN.md; report only correctness gaps")

# fan-out over a file list, tightly scoped
while read -r f; do
  claude -p "Migrate $f from unittest to pytest. Reply OK or FAIL: <reason>." \
    --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(pytest $f)" --permission-mode dontAsk
done < files.txt
takeaways: Use git worktrees so parallel sessions don't edit the same checkout
A fresh-context reviewer catches what the writer missed; limit it to real gaps
Fan out with `claude -p` or `/batch`; gate unattended runs with `/goal` or a Stop hook
pitfalls: Running the full fan-out before testing the prompt on two or three files, multiplying one mistake hundreds of times.

quiz.q: Why use a separate session or subagent to review Claude's implementation?
options: Reviews must use a different model
A fresh context isn't biased toward code it just wrote
The writer session can't read diffs
quiz.explain: Independent context evaluates the result on its own terms.

quiz.q: What makes parallel Claude sessions safe to run on one repository?
options: Running them in the same folder
Git worktrees giving each its own checkout and branch
quiz.explain: Worktrees isolate file changes per session.
